samples.ref: ततः स गत्वा यिहूदीयान् अवदद् यीशु र्माम् अरोगिणम् अकार्षीत्।
samples.raw:
<thinking>
Sentence: "The man departed, and told the Jews that it was Jesus, which had made him whole."

Structure: man departed (past), told Jews (past), it was Jesus (nominal clause), which had made him whole (past passive/agent).

Parasmaipada. जैसुः? "Jesus" in Sanskrit: जैसुः (jāsuḥ) is the standard form. Actually जैसुः is used for Jesus in the sense of "he who is" (divine). Also जिसुः. For the man, "he who was made whole" — जैसुः.

Departed: अपरता (aparata) — but that's for अपरति. For man: अपरत् (aparat). Actually अपरत् is the past of अपरति (to go away). Yes, "aparati" → "aparata" (3rd sg), "aparat" (1st sg).

Told: अपठ् (aparati → aparati; past: aparati, aparata, aparant). So "aparati" for 3rd sg.

So: अपरत् + अपरति + जैसुः + अपरत्.

Wait, "it was Jesus" — the nominal clause: जैसुः (with अपरत् agreeing). Then "which had made him whole" — passive of कर्मणि: अपरत् (aparat).

So अपरत् अपरति जैसुः अपरत्.

Sandhi: अपरत् + अपरति = अपरतपरति? No, the first is अपरत् (a-p-a-r-a-t), second अपरति (a-p-a-r-a-t-i). No sandhi. Then जैसुः + अपरत् = जैसुः अपरत्.

Result: अपरत अपरति जैसुः अपरत्.

Hmm, but should the final be अपरत् or अपरत? Ending in अपरत् — but the sentence ends in "him" subject, so it's a full sentence ending in अपरत्. Yes.

Actually, is there a rule: अपरत् + अपरति → अपरतपरति? No, since the first ends in अ and the second in अ, no sandhi (a + a = a).

So अपरत अपरति जैसुः अपरत्.
</thinking>

<translation>अपरत अपरति जैसुः अपरत्</translation>

So आमहे तिष्ठाः, अस्ति आप्यायाः (that I may preach there also) — आप्यायाः is the passive of आप्यायति (to preach). अस्ति आप्यायाः.

samples.raw:

Parasmaipada, third person singular: ग्रन्थयति / पुस्तकयति.

The verb is "to spread" — व्यक्ति... Actually the verb used is "to spread" (स्प्रेड) but in Sanskrit, the standard form is ग्रन्थयति (from ग्रन्थ् + अयति). The verb अयति comes from अय (to spread) — ग्रन्थयति = fragrance spreads.

So ग्रन्थयति. Alternatively पुस्तकयति.

Sandhi: ग्रन्थ् + अयति = ग्रन्थयति.
</thinking>

Sentence: "So, it is to be kept outside of the installation folder."

Structure: "So" (adverb) + subject "it" + verb "is to be kept" + location "outside of the installation folder."

In Sanskrit, the passive/impersonal construction: त्वया आश्रयः... Actually for "it is to be kept", the passive form uses यक् (श्यन्?) — the standard: कर्मणि/भावे यक् is added, and the subject is neuter singular. So "it" → ते? No — in passive, the subject is always neuter singular (ता). So "it is to be kept" → तेर्वा? Let's think: passive of "to keep" = कार्यते (कर्ता → कार्यते). So "it is to be kept" = तेर्वा? No, that's not right.

Actually the passive of "it is to be kept" — the subject is "it" (the thing to be kept), which is neuter singular. Passive: तेर्वा? The standard translation: "तेर्वा" no. Let's recall: कार्यते = "it is to be kept". So the form is कार्यते, with ते ending (from ता → ते by तित आत्मनेपदम्... actually ता → ते by "तित आत्मनेपदम्" rule: तित् becomes ते). So "it is to be kept" = कार्यते.

Now the location: "outside of the installation folder" — आत्मनेपद with अन्त्यात्... The adverb "outside" in passive: अन्त्यात् आत्मनेपदे (7.2.11?) — rule: अन्त्यात् आत्मनेपदे (7.2.11) — after a तित् (short त्) ending, आत् is replaced by आत्मनेपद. So कार्यते + आत्मनेपद → कार्यते + आत्मनेपद = कार्यते + आत्मनेपद... hmm.

Actually the rule: अन्त्यात् आत्मनेपदे — "आत्" which follows a तित् ending becomes आत्मनेपद. So कार्यते + आत्मनेपद = कार्यते + आत्मनेपद = कार्यते + आत्मनेपद → कार्यते + आत्मनेपद = कार्यते + आत्मनेपद... the आत्मनेपद form is ते, so कार्यते + आते = कार्यताते? Hmm, that gives कार्यताते which is "it is to be kept outside" — that's the standard passive of "it is to be kept outside" = कार्यताते. Yes! कार्यताते.

Now the "installation folder" — आश्रयः? The folder is "installation" (निर्वाण/स्थापन). In Sanskrit, "installation folder" = आश्रय (आश्रयः). So "it is to be kept outside of the installation folder" = कार्यताते आश्रये.

Hmm, but is आश्रय the right term? आश्रयः "a place of refuge". Yes, commonly used for software installation folders. So कार्यताते आश्रये.

Wait — but should the passive be कार्यते or कार्यताते? The standard: "it is to be kept" → कार्यते; "it is to be kept outside" → कार्यताते. Yes.

Also, should the ending be आश्रये (with आत्मनेपद आत्मनेपद) — कार्यताते + आश्रये = कार्यताते आश्रये. Yes.

Also consider: is there a rule that आश्रयः's आ becomes... no. Also, "it" — is it कार्यताते or कार्यताते? Fine.

Also, should the sentence begin with अन्त्यात्... no, that's the rule.

So translation: कार्यताते आश्रये.

Hmm, but should the passive form use the same ते ending? Yes, कार्यताते आश्रये.

Actually, wait — is there a rule for आश्रयः: "आश्रये" — आश्रयः is neuter singular, so आत्मनेपद ते → आश्रये. Yes.

Final: कार्यताते आश्रये.

Sentence: "And then click on Save at the bottom of the page."

Structure: And then + click on + Save + at the bottom of the page.

In Sanskrit, "and then" → अन्त (anta) with अट् augment: अन्त. Actually "then" is तस् → अन्त (with अट् augment: अ + अन्त = अन्त). So "and then" = अन्त.

Save → सेव् (from सेव्, "to save"). So च्लिक्ष्णा सेव्.

At the bottom of the page → पृष्ठे अन्त्ये / अन्त्यपृष्ठे. Standard: अन्त्यपृष्ठे.

So: अन्त च्लिक्ष्णा सेव् अन्त्यपृष्ठे.

Sandhi: च्लिक्ष्णा + सेव् → च्लिक्ष्णासेव्. Yes.

Final: अन्त च्लिक्ष्णासेव अन्त्यपृष्ठे.
</thinking>

samples.ref: वामपार्श्वस्य नेविगेशन् मेन्यू मध्ये Calculus  कोर्स् नुदन्तु ।
samples.raw:
<thinking>
Sentence: "Click on the Calculus course in the left navigation menu."

This is a command, so it takes the imperative form. The verb "click" — in Sanskrit, for such instructions, the verb is often "kriyā" form... Actually in these translation exercises, the standard approach: use the ātmanepada imperative of the verb "to click" — but there's no specific verb; typically "kriyā" is used. However, for such instructional texts, the translation uses the ātmanepada imperative of "kriyā" (kriyāte → kriyāte; imperative kriyātām, kriyātām).

Actually many such datasets use "kriyā" with ātmanepada endings. The left navigation menu → "vamāṃ" (vamāṃ) — the left side is "vamāṃ" (from "vam" + ām). So "kriyā vamāṃ caṣṭāṃ caṣṭām caṣṭaḥ caṣṭa".

Let's construct: kriyā + vamāṃ + caṣṭāṃ + caṣṭām + caṣṭaḥ + caṣṭa.
- kriyā + vamāṃ → vamāṃ (no sandhi since vamāṃ ends in ām, and kriyā ends in ā, ā + ām = ām by sandhi "āṭaś ca" → ām). So kriyāvamāṃ.
- kriyā + caṣṭām → kriyācaṣṭām.
- kriyā + caṣṭaḥ → kriyācaṣṭaḥ.
- kriyā + caṣṭa → kriyācaṣṭa.

So kriyāvamāṃ caṣṭāṃ caṣṭām caṣṭaḥ caṣṭa.

Hmm, but is there a rule about "caṣṭaḥ caṣṭa" — the final "caṣṭa" with ātmanepada ending "caṣṭa" (from "ta" → "caṣṭa" by "ṭa caṣṭaḥ" rule: ṭa → caṣṭa). Yes.

So the translation: क्रियावमां चष्टां चष्टाम् चष्टा चष्ट.

Check sandhi: kriyā + vamāṃ = kriyāvamāṃ (ā + ām → ām). Then caṣṭāṃ: kriyāvamāṃcaṣṭāṃ → kriyāvamāṃcaṣṭāṃ. Then caṣṭām: kriyāvamāṃcaṣṭāṃcaṣṭām. Then caṣṭaḥ: kriyāvamāṃcaṣṭāṃcaṣṭāmcaṣṭaḥ. Then caṣṭa: kriyāvamāṃcaṣṭāṃcaṣṭāmcaṣṭa.

Devanagari: क्रियावमां चष्टां चष्टाम् चष्ट चष्ट.
